topic: Bayes' Theorem and the Logic of Independence
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students

sections.title: Introduction: The Intuition of Independence
sections.content: Define 'Independence' as the scenario where one event occurring does not change the probability of another. Visually represent this using a 'Probability Square' where the area of intersection equals the product of individual side lengths.
sections.example: Flipping a coin while a cat meows. The cat meowing doesn't change the 50% chance of heads; these are independent events.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Conditional Probability & The Shrinking Universe
sections.content: Introduce P(A|B) — the probability of A occurring *given* B has happened. Graphically, show the 'Sample Space' (a large rectangle) shrinking to only the area of 'Event B'. The new probability is the 'A and B' intersection divided by the 'B' area.
sections.example: In a deck of cards, the probability of drawing a King is 4/52. But if we *know* the card is a Face Card (Event B), our 'universe' shrinks to 12 cards, making the probability 4/12.

sections.title: The Core: Deriving Bayes' Theorem
sections.content: Explain that Bayes' Theorem is just a way to 'flip' conditional probability. Use an animation to show the relationship between P(A|B) and P(B|A). Present the formula: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B). Highlight that this is how we update our beliefs based on new evidence.
sections.example: A 'Robot Sentry' sees a blurry shape. It knows the 'Prior' (how likely a thief is) and the 'Likelihood' (how often a thief looks like that shape) to calculate the 'Posterior' (the chance it's actually a thief).

sections.title: Step-by-Step Application: The Rare Dragon Test
sections.content: Apply the theorem to a classic 'False Positive' scenario using a flow-chart or tree diagram. This demonstrates why a positive test result doesn't always mean the condition is present, especially if the base rate (prior) is low.
sections.example: A Dragon-Detector is 99% accurate. Dragons are rare (1 in 1,000). If the alarm sounds, Bayes' Theorem shows there is only a ~9% chance it's a real dragon, because the 1% false alarm rate on 999 non-dragons outweighs the 99% true hit on 1 dragon.

sections.title: Conclusion: Independence vs. Bayesian Updating
sections.content: Summarize the key difference: Independence means new information is irrelevant. Bayes' Theorem proves that when events *are* dependent, new evidence allows us to update our certainty mathematically. End with a visual recap of the 'Probability Square' vs. the 'Shrinking Universe'.
sections.example: If the Dragon-Detector alarm is independent of dragons (it's broken), the probability remains 1/1,000. Because it's dependent, we use Bayes to update our 1/1,000 belief to 9%.
